questions.q: Why do servers talk to PostgreSQL through a connection pool instead of opening a connection per request?
questions.explain: Reusing a few open connections removes the setup cost from every request and keeps the total under max_connections.
options: PostgreSQL only accepts pooled connections
Each connection is a server process that costs time to open (network, authentication, TLS) and memory while open, and the server caps how many can exist
Pools make queries run in parallel on one connection
Pools encrypt the connection

questions.q: PostgreSQL allows 100 connections. You run 6 app servers, each with new pg.Pool({ max: 20 }). What happens at peak traffic?
questions.explain: Pools do not know about each other. Instances × pool size (plus migrations, cron and people) must stay below max_connections, or you need a pooler such as PgBouncer.
options: Nothing: pools share connections across servers
The servers try to open up to 120 connections and some fail with "sorry, too many clients already" (53300)
PostgreSQL raises its limit automatically
Each pool shrinks itself to fit

questions.q: The lesson's pool of 20 finished 20 pg_sleep(0.2) queries faster than a pool of 5. Why doesn't that mean "bigger pools are always faster"?
questions.explain: A database server with 8 cores cannot execute 200 CPU-bound queries faster than 20. Size pools from the database's capacity, then measure.
options: Because pg_sleep is not allowed in production
Sleeping uses no CPU or disk; real queries compete for a fixed number of cores and disks, so beyond a point more connections only add switching and memory
Because pools larger than 10 are refused
Because a larger pool uses more JavaScript memory

questions.q: A site works for an hour after each restart, then every request hangs, while the database looks idle. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explain: A leaked client never returns. Once all are leaked, every request waits for a connection. Release in finally, set connectionTimeoutMillis so the failure is loud, and monitor the pool's waiting count.
options: The database ran out of disk
A code path acquires a pooled client and never releases it (for example on an error), until the pool is empty
Too many indexes
The pool's max is too large

questions.q: What does PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode change?
questions.explain: It lets hundreds of app processes use a database that should hold only dozens of connections. The catch: session state (set, session advisory locks, listen) does not stick to a client between transactions.
options: It caches query results
A real server connection is lent to a client only for the length of a transaction, so many client connections share few server connections
It makes every statement its own transaction
It replicates writes to replicas

questions.q: Why did renaming phone to phone_number in one migration break checkouts, although the new code used the new name correctly?
questions.explain: For some minutes, old and new versions share one database. Every schema state must work with every version running at that moment, which a one-step rename cannot.
options: Renames are not supported by PostgreSQL
During the rolling deploy, servers still running the old code queried phone, which no longer existed
The migration ran in the wrong transaction
The new code was cached

questions.q: What is the correct order for an expand and contract column rename?
questions.explain: Each step is compatible with every version running at that moment. The old column is removed only when no running code uses it.
options: Drop the old column, add the new one, deploy new code
Deploy new code, then add the new column
Add the new column and keep both in sync, backfill, deploy code that uses the new column, then (in a later deploy) drop the old one
Rename the column and restart all servers at the same instant

questions.q: An instant alter table … add column is waiting for its lock behind a long report transaction. Why do simple selects on the table start hanging too?
questions.explain: Lock requests are served in order. The migration's request conflicts with everything, so every later query waits behind it. lock_timeout makes the migration give up instead of freezing the table.
options: Because add column rewrites the table
They queue behind the waiting ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock request, which itself waits for the report
Because the report locked the whole database
Because the pool is too small

questions.q: What does set lock_timeout = '2s' before a migration achieve?
questions.explain: It limits waiting for locks, not the work itself. A failed attempt is harmless and retryable; a frozen table is an outage.
options: The migration finishes within 2 seconds
If the migration cannot get its lock within 2 seconds it fails (55P03) instead of blocking everyone behind it; you retry it later
Other sessions give up their locks after 2 seconds
It releases the lock 2 seconds after the migration starts

questions.q: What does adding a check constraint with not valid do?
questions.explain: Adding the constraint becomes quick, and the full scan happens later in validate constraint, under a lock that does not block writes. Existing bad rows can be fixed in between.
options: It adds a constraint that is never enforced
It enforces the rule on new and changed rows immediately, but skips checking existing rows until validate constraint runs
It checks only existing rows
It disables the constraint during migrations

questions.q: How do you make an existing column not null on a large, busy table without a long exclusive lock?
questions.explain: A plain set not null scans the whole table under an exclusive lock. PostgreSQL 12+ skips that scan when a validated check constraint already proves no nulls exist.
options: alter table … alter column … set not null directly; it is always instant
Add check (col is not null) not valid, validate it, then set not null, which can use the validated check instead of scanning
Drop and recreate the table
It is impossible

questions.q: Why backfill ten million rows in batches of a few thousand instead of one update?
questions.explain: Small batches commit often, can be paused, resumed after a crash, throttled, and watched. Each touches few rows for a short time.
options: One update cannot change more than a million rows
A single huge update is one long transaction: it locks every row it touched until the end, floods WAL to replicas, and loses all its work if it fails or is cancelled
Batches use less disk in total
Because triggers only fire in batches

questions.q: A migration that ran in production last week has a bug. What should you do?
questions.explain: Databases that already ran the old version will never run an edited one, and down scripts can destroy data written since. Fix forward; the checksum check refuses in-place edits.
options: Edit the migration file and rerun it
Run the migration's down script, then fix it
Write a new migration that corrects the problem
Delete its row from schema_migrations and run it again

questions.q: Which rows belong in a seed that runs on every deploy, including production?
questions.explain: Reference data is part of the application's correct behaviour. Development data must never reach production, and test fixtures belong to the tests that use them.
options: Fake customers and orders for demos
The rows a particular test needs
Reference data the application needs everywhere, such as delivery zones or order statuses
A copy of yesterday's production data
None: seeds never run in production

questions.q: Why must a deploy-time seed be idempotent?
questions.explain: insert … on conflict (natural key) do update or do nothing makes a seed safe to repeat. Plain inserts duplicate rows or fail on the second run.
options: So it runs faster
Because it runs on every deploy: running it again must give the same result, with no duplicates and no errors
So it can be rolled back
Because PostgreSQL requires it

questions.q: A seed inserts child categories with parent_id = 3, a generated id copied from the developer's laptop. What is the problem?
questions.explain: Seeds must refer to rows by stable natural keys (a slug or code) and look up ids inside the insert, as the lesson's tree seed does.
options: Nothing, ids are the same everywhere
Generated ids differ between databases, so on another database the children may point at the wrong parent or none
Foreign keys cannot reference generated ids
The seed will be too slow

questions.q: Why is a streaming replica not a backup?
questions.explain: Replication protects against losing a server. Backups (and point-in-time recovery) protect against losing data through mistakes, which replicas faithfully reproduce.
options: Replicas are slower
It copies every change within moments, including a delete without where or a bad migration
Replicas cannot be read
It is a backup, as long as it is synchronous

questions.q: You take a pg_dump every night at 02:00. At 17:30 someone deletes all orders. With only the dump, what is lost?
questions.explain: A dump is a snapshot. Your recovery point objective (RPO) with nightly dumps is up to 24 hours. Point-in-time recovery, from a base backup plus archived WAL, can restore to 17:29:59.
options: Nothing
Every change made between 02:00 and 17:30: that gap is the recovery point
Only the deleted orders
The whole database

questions.q: What proves that your backups work?
questions.explain: Backups fail in quiet ways: wrong database, missing permissions, corrupted files, an encryption key nobody has. Only a restore proves a backup, and it also measures your recovery time.
options: The backup job exits with code 0
The backup file is larger than yesterday's
Regularly restoring the latest backup into a scratch database and running checks against it
The cloud provider's dashboard shows a green tick

questions.q: With default (asynchronous) streaming replication, what can a read from a replica return right after a commit on the primary?
questions.explain: The primary does not wait for replicas, so they lag by milliseconds normally and by much more under load. Synchronous replication removes the lag for confirmed commits at the cost of slower commits.
options: An error
Data from just before that commit, if the replica has not replayed it yet
Uncommitted data
Always the newest data

questions.q: Ada pays for an order and is redirected to her order page, which reads from a replica and shows "unpaid". Which guarantee is broken, and what is a simple fix?
questions.explain: Users expect to see their own changes. Sticky reads after a write, or waiting until the replica has replayed the write's WAL position, keeps that promise while other reads still use replicas.
options: Durability; use synchronous commit
Read-your-writes; send a user's reads to the primary for a short time after that user writes
Atomicity; wrap the page in a transaction
Isolation; use serializable

questions.explain: After the rename, any code still using title fails with 42703 (undefined column). 42P01 would be an undefined table.

questions.q: During the expand step, an old server inserts using only the old column. What does this print?
questions.explain: A before trigger can change the row being written. Whichever column a version writes, the trigger fills the other, so old and new servers both see complete data.
options: An error: a trigger cannot change the row

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: New rows are checked at once, so product 3 is refused. Updating product 1 to a valid price is fine. Validation scans the old rows and finds product 2 with a price of 0, so it fails until that row is fixed.
options: ok ok 23514
23514 ok ok
ok ok ok

questions.q: How many batches does this backfill run?
questions.explain: 1,000 + 1,000 + 500 rows. The fourth query finds no rows left and ends the loop without counting a batch.

questions.q: The seed runs twice. What does this print?
questions.explain: do nothing keeps the existing ABJ row; do update overwrites LAG with the new value (excluded is the row that was proposed). Neither duplicates nor fails.
options: An error on the second run: duplicate key

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each attempted insert draws the next identity value before the conflict is detected, and a skipped row does not give it back. That is why seeds must never depend on generated ids.
options: 1:rice 2:oil 5:beans
1:rice 2:oil 3:beans
1:rice 2:oil 3:rice 4:rice 5:beans
3:rice 2:oil 5:beans

questions.q: A migration tool wraps every migration in a transaction. What does this print?
questions.explain: A concurrent index build commits several internal transactions of its own, so it refuses to run inside yours. Migration tools need a way to run such a migration outside a transaction.
options:
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block
[ 'orders_customer_idx', 'orders_pkey' ]
[ 'orders_customer_idx', 'orders_pkey' ]

CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block
[ 'orders_pkey' ]

deadlock detected
[ 'orders_customer_idx', 'orders_pkey' ]

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The backup captured 300 orders. The 50 orders written after it are not in it (that is the recovery point), and the later delete is not either, which is the point of having it.

questions.q: A pool with one connection. What does this print?
questions.explain: All three call acquire before any await resumes: A takes the only connection (but logs "runs" only after its await), B and C find none and queue. Then A runs and releases to B, which releases to C, in queue order.
options: B waits, C waits, A runs, B runs, C runs
A runs, B runs, C runs
A runs, B waits, B runs, C waits, C runs
A runs, B waits, C waits, B runs, C runs

questions.q: Write poolPerInstance({ maxConnections, reserved, fixed, instances }): the largest pool size each app instance may use so that instances × pool + fixed + reserved stays within maxConnections. Return 0 if even that is impossible.
questions.explain: Work from the database's limit down, and round down. At 30 instances each pool may hold only 5, which is a sign to cap scaling or add PgBouncer.

questions.q: Write an idempotent seed on a Map. seed(table, rows, mode) inserts each row by its code; for an existing code, "nothing" keeps the stored row and "update" replaces it. Running the same seed twice must not change the result.
questions.explain: With "nothing", existing rows (including the hand-edited ABJ fee) are kept and only KAN is new, like on conflict do nothing. Copying the row ({ ...row }) keeps the seed's input from being changed through the table.

questions.q: Plan a keyset backfill. Write batches(maxId, size) that returns [from, to] id ranges (inclusive) covering 1 to maxId, each at most size ids, for queries like where id between $1 and $2.
questions.explain: Ranges on the primary key use its index and never re-scan finished work, unlike repeatedly searching for is null rows. Commit after each range, and you can resume from the last finished one.

questions.q: Keep read-your-writes with replicas. WAL positions (LSNs) look like "0/7000A28": two hexadecimal numbers. Write lsnToBigInt(lsn) (high part × 232 + low part) and pickReplica(replicas, needed) returning the name of the first replica whose replayed LSN is at or past needed, or "primary".
questions.explain: After a write, the app notes pg_current_wal_lsn(); a replica is safe for that user once its pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() has passed it. Comparing LSNs as strings would be wrong ("0/9" > "0/10"), hence the numeric conversion.

questions.q: Check a migration plan. Each schema step lists the columns that exist; each app version lists the columns it uses. Write broken(step, running, versions) returning the running versions that use a column the step does not have.
questions.explain: The one-step rename breaks v1 while it is still running. The expand step keeps both columns, so both versions work, and the contract step is safe only because v1 is no longer running.
questions.expected:
rename in one go [ 'v1' ]
expand []
contract []

questions.q: Decide which nightly backups to keep: the newest 7 dailies, plus the newest backup of each of the 4 most recent weeks that are not already kept. Weeks are numbered Math.floor(day / 7). Write keep(days) for a list of backup day numbers and return the kept days, sorted descending.
questions.explain: Seven dailies cover days 34 to 40 (weeks 4 and 5). The newest backups of the next four weeks are days 27, 20, 13 and 6. Retention rules like this bound storage cost while keeping older restore points; whatever you keep, restore-test it.

questions.q: Compute data loss. Given backup times and the time of an accident (all as "HH:MM" on one day), write lossMinutes(backups, accident): minutes between the last backup at or before the accident and the accident. Return null if there is no such backup.
questions.explain: With one nightly dump, an accident at 17:30 loses 15.5 hours of orders; four dumps a day cut it to 5.5 hours. Point-in-time recovery reduces it to seconds, which is why production databases archive WAL.

questions.q: What do you gain and lose by making replication synchronous (synchronous_standby_names)?
questions.explain: Asynchronous replication risks losing the last moments of commits on failover; synchronous replication trades commit latency (and availability, if standbys are down) for zero loss. Many teams use one synchronous standby and more asynchronous ones.
options: You gain faster commits and lose read capacity
A confirmed commit is also on a standby, so failover loses nothing; but every commit waits for the standby, and stalls if no standby answers
Replicas can accept writes
Nothing changes except the log format

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: set local lasts until the end of the transaction, so the migration's timeout cannot leak into other work on a pooled connection. A plain set sticks to the session, which is exactly what breaks behind a transaction-pooling PgBouncer.
options: 2s 0 5s
2s 2s 5s

At 4000 the difference is negative, which is less than 1000, so a clock that goes backwards (or a read that started before the write) also goes to the primary; at 6000 exactly 1000 ms have passed, so Ada is back on the replica. Tunde never wrote, so all his reads use the replica.
